utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I appear to prosecute with Susan Somers, Kenneth Scott, Patrick Lopez-Terres, and Rodney Dixon; case manager, Alinde Verhaag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the Kordic Defence, Your Honour, we have here Turner Smith; my colleague, Mitko Naumovski; Robert Stein; my colleague from our Fairfax office, Steve Sayers; and Jadranka Berkic, who has not been before the court before but is a paralegal who will be our courtroom assistant; and Ksenija Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I am an attorney-at-law from Croatia, from Njivice. Let me introduce my co-counsel, Mr. Goran Mikulicic, who is here for the first time with me, and my legal assistant, Mr. Vladimir Pavlekovic, who was here previously as a co-counsel. At the same time, I am asking the Court permission to have a legal assistant with us in the courtroom for the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be no need during the trial to mention the appearances again unless lead counsel is away or there is a substantial change in any of the legal teams; otherwise, we will assume the appearances are as today. I am going to turn to the accused next to ensure that they can hear the proceedings in a language which they understand. Mr. Kordic, can you hear the proceedings all right? THE ACCUSED KORDIC: (Interpretation) Your Honours, good morning. Thank you for having asked. I understand everything and I can follow the trial today normally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez? THE ACCUSED CERKEZ: (Interpretation) Honourable President, Your Honours, thank you. I am able to understand everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I shan't again during the trial ask you if you can hear and understand the proceedings. If, for some reason, you can't, then indicate immediately. If necessary, speak out. So at any stage, let the Court know if you can't follow what's being said. If you would like to sit down? Mr. Nice, if I could address you? The matter clearly is listed for opening, and that should be dealt with as quickly as possible, but there are some preliminary matters which are outstanding which I wish to deal with now, but by way of various rulings and announcements. The first matter, in fact, concerns the Defence, and it relates to the seating of the accused. In fact, the application was made by Mr. Kovacic at the pre-trial hearing, for the accused to be seated next to their counsel, and I said then that we would consider the matter and rule on it. We have done that. We have ruled that the accused should remain where they are. This has always been the practice in this Tribunal, which we think should be continued in this case, also for security reasons. The next ruling concerns the proceedings generally, and we have decided that all motions during the course of the trial should be made orally. Written motions will only be entertained with the leave of the Trial Chamber or at its request. The reason we make this ruling is in order to achieve a more expeditious trial, in order to save public time and money. A written motion has, for instance, first of all, to be deposited with the registry, it then has to be translated, same thing has to happen to any response, and the same with a written decision. Oral motions or rulings can, of course, be dealt with immediately, and there is a record in the form of the transcript. The other matter which does concern the Prosecution is this, that you have provided a witness list, but there is no time estimate attached to it as far as I see, and that is required by Rule 73 bis; that is, that in relation to each Prosecution witness, there should be a time estimate of the length of his examination-in-chief. Now, Mr. Nice, can you undertake to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can, of course, undertake to provide an estimate. I think I discussed the matter with Mr. Smith on an earlier occasion, and I think we actually agreed that until the case is under way, it is very difficult to estimate, for any particular type of witness, how long the witness will take, but certainly we will provide an estimate, and, of course, our calling up of future witnesses is based on a very approximate estimate that we have already made of how long witnesses will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, seven days then for that. There is one matter of housekeeping, and that concerns the week beginning the 26th of April where it is possible that we shall not be sitting in the mornings; that is because of a relisting of other cases, in one of which I am sitting in the mornings of that week, if it is listed. But we will give you further details when they are available. Mr. Nice, as far as the other matters are concerned, it would seem to me more convenient to deal with them after the opening. I have in mind applications in relation to protective measures for witnesses and also problems that have arisen due to the translation of witness statements, but I anticipate that these will require the hearing and consideration of submissions, some of which may be in closed session, and therefore it is more convenient to deal with that after we have heard the opening. Are there any matters before you open which you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only one. In the course of my opening, I am going to be taking Your Honours through quite a number of the bundle of core documents that were submitted with the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. Perhaps that will be the most helpful way to familiarise the Court with the issues in this case. I will, of course, not be reading any documents slavishly line by line, and insofar as I shall be reading them at all, it will be in English. I know that professional judges can move through documents, even if they are not familiar with them, frequently at a reasonable speed, and I am not inclined at present, unless otherwise advised, to use the ELMO to put documents on on a regular basis. I would, of course, be sensitive to any different view that the Court takes, bearing in mind its duty to make these public proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I suspect it is a matter for you how you deal with it. I would have thought some of the documents should certainly be displayed so that the public can see them and follow what's being said. But I leave that entirely for you to decide and make your own choice. How long do you anticipate being in opening?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's always very difficult, but I should think I'll probably consume the morning. I had originally thought it would be shorter, but I suspect it will be the morning. Until I see the speed at which collectively we go through the documents, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Chamber will take the usual break at 11.15, 20 minutes' break. There is one matter for the Defence, and it is this, that the Rules provide, of course, that the Defence can make a statement, if they wish, an opening statement, following the Prosecution opening. Do counsel wish to avail themselves of that opportunity, or do they wish to reserve their opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will, for the Kordic Defence, reserve our opening statement, and we have several matters of a preliminary nature that I think are best taken up after the opening statement when Your Honour is examining the question involving translations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, we also based our decision on Rule 84, that is to say, to make our statement after the Prosecutor's statement. There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is interpretation. Can everyone hear us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you won't be making a statement today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As the Court will know, on the morning of the 16th of April of 1993, the small village of Ahmici, lying close to Vitez, was turned red by the flames of its houses that were burnt to the ground and by the blood of its innocent inhabitants who were killed in a massacre, killed by those favouring the interests of the Croats against the Muslims. That appalling crime, of course, as we know in this Tribunal -- and in numerical terms by no means the worst that this Tribunal has to deal with, but nevertheless an appalling crime -- is one of the matters charged against these two men, Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez, and its seriousness could make it the focus, the centre of gravity of this case and could concentrate attention on it, but that would not be, in our respectful submission, a correct or an easy approach to this case. For what is said against these two men is that they took part in a long-term and a geographically widespread persecution of Muslims in the centre of Bosnia, and that persecution was varied in its effects. It started at one level and descended until the depths of the attack on Ahmici and on other villages that same night, and continued thereafter with another serious coda in the killings at Stupni Do, until it ended -- indeed, it was effectively just switched off -- at the Washington Agreement. So that this is a case where careful attention will have to be paid to a long course of conduct. Similarly, this is not a case where the Prosecution suggests that there wasn't wrong and there wasn't crime committed by other parties, indeed, by all sides, and this is not a case where the Prosecution suggests that these defendants or either of them embarked on what they did with an initial intention to commit crime or monstrous acts. This is a case where people found themselves in conflict, and of course the conflict started by the Serbs, something outside the control of the parties to this particular case. They found themselves in conflict, and it may be that the Court will, in due course, consider whether it was a combination of their individual strengths and weaknesses, perhaps their inadequacies and their ambitions, that led in one case or the other to their having vested in them power and authority that might never have come to them in well-ordered society. But of course the circumstances of war are different, and once the power and authority of the type we shall see did vest in these defendants, was with them, it would be both difficult to surrender or to have taken away, and it might in the very nature of things be both addictive and corrupting, and by whatever process men find themselves in positions of power and responsibility, if they abuse the power and fail to discharge the responsibility, they must face the consequences of their actions and failures. But again, the Court will need, no doubt with great care, to examine the long-term history of the actions of these men, and particularly of the first defendant, Kordic. If I use his surname for brevity, I hope no one will mind; it's to save time, and it shows no disrespect. The Court will need to look at things long term, no doubt asking itself from time to time what was the state of mind of this man, what were his then-revealed intentions and aspirations, were the things that he said -- and there were things that were favourable to the Muslims -- were they sincere or otherwise? Therefore, just as with the persecution campaign itself, there is no simple answer, there is no simple approach to this case, because there is no simple, single issue. So it must be that the Court will have to look at material starting at the beginning and working its way through to the end. Recognising that, we've presented our material to the Court, so far as we've been able, and we will call evidence so far as we are able, in a chronological order, for we judge that will assist the Court more than having the material in any other way. Before I turn to the facts themselves, we have provided a small clip of maps that we thought might be of some assistance to the Court in opening. I've shown them to Mr. Smith, and I don't believe there is any objection to them being made available. Can I make them available through the usher to the Court now? As to numbering of exhibits, and in respect of this exhibit perhaps alone, can I ask that its numbering be deferred, for this reason: An exhibit list has been prepared; there have been some problems with the final version of it and getting the computer numbers right, and if we could postpone giving this small exhibit a number until perhaps the session that will follow my opening address, I would be very grateful. The maps probably reveal to the Court no more than it already knows, the first map simply showing the former Yugoslavia and the location of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one of its constituent federations, the second map showing the relevant opstina boundaries outlined in yellow with which in this indictment the Court will be concerned. Starting at the bottom of the yellow markings, Novi Travnik -- I'm so sorry. Is it missing from Judge Robinson's ... I'm sorry, it should always be possible to tell whether the Court is with one with the document, but the television screens sometimes get in the way. Novi Travnik, towards the left, Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak in a line, Zenica above, and Zepce above that, with Vares separated and to the right. The third map, viewed the other way -- and I'm afraid the internal boundaries are rather stronger than one would like and tend to a degree to mask the roads and the towns; nevertheless, we can see the important towns all marked on this map, starting at the left with Travnik, and underneath Travnik, on one of the dividing black lines, Pucarevo, which I think is to be referred to in this trial more often as Novi Travnik. To the right of that -- and I trust the Court can see that; it's a little hard to see -- to the right of that, Vitez. Further to the right, Busovaca. Then above that, Zenica and Zepce, and then over to the right, the municipality of Vares. I needn't trouble the Court probably at all in opening with the town maps, but they will be available for use later. I think they are more likely to be useful with individual witnesses at a later stage. Bosnia has a long and indeed fascinating history. In due course, historians will be called, and insofar as it's helpful to the Tribunal, evidence of the relevant history will be before you, and I make this point about our role as prosecutors in this case. Our role as prosecutors is to lay before this Tribunal the evidence that covers the topic, and to advance the arguments that justify conviction on this indictment. Those we perceive to be our duties. So far as opening this case is concerned, I need for purposes of history go no further back than 1939, and on page 1 of the chronological schedule that was an attachment to the pre-trial brief, the Court will know that between 1939 and 1941, by an agreement, the state of Croatia was enlarged, perhaps to the largest size it has ever been historically, by the incorporation or creation of an area called the Banovina, and that enlarged state features significantly in what is to follow. The Tribunal will then know that there was another government between 1941 and 1945. It went by the name of the Independent State of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Smith, it's a bit early for an objection. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for taking up your time, but my duty compels me to object to references to the government during this time. We have in our reply brief indicated that we thought that government is irrelevant. It was a government answering to an independent and different country at this time and not involved in this matter. And we believe it is highly prejudicial under Rule 89(A). It was put into the Prosecutor's chronology. We objected in our restatement of the chronology. We believe that it is an unnecessary and irrelevant and highly objectional reference, Your Honour. (Trial Chamber deliberates).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Smith, we're against you at this stage. The Prosecutor must be entitled to outline his case as he thinks fit. If there is evidence to which you object on the grounds of being prejudicial or something of the sort, of course we will rule on it. But this isn't an appropriate time to give a ruling of that sort. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, I've said all that I need to say and wanted to say about that government at this stage. I will refer to it briefly again later on. We can then move right up to the 1990s. The focus of our first attention is not on Bosnia, but in Croatia. Of course, as the Court will know from its prereading of papers, this case has as one of its elements the fact that there was close contact between President Tudjman of Croatia, or others in Zagreb, and those with whom the Court is concerned in this case. It will also know that, of course, the contribution by Croatia of armed forces in the matter with which you are concerned is an element that goes to proving an international armed conflict in this case, but I'll return to that if necessary in the opening or certainly later in the evidence. In 1989, in Croatia, the HDZ, a nationalist Croatian party, was formed, and Franjo Tudjman was the leader. He drafted the programme for the party which was nationalistic in tone and asserting the right of Croatian people to self-determination within their historic borders. It may be that the proper inference to draw is that "historic borders" referred back to that enlarged state, the Banovina, between 1939 and 1941, to which I have already referred. In April and May of 1990, in Croatia, multiparty elections occurred, and Tudjman became president, with a man called Stipe Mesic as prime minister. Following its successes in Croatia, the HDZ as a party extended its activities into Bosnia and Herzegovina and indeed founded a party with that name on the 18th of August in Sarajevo. We can pass on the chronology to the second sheet. The goals of that party, the local party, the Bosnian party, were stated to be continued respect for continued coexistence of different ethnic groups in Bosnia, but those expressed intentions will have always to be put beside some clear expressions that were to be forthcoming, as the Court may decide, of an intention to be part of a greater Croatia. If we look at page 2 of the chronology, the Court will observe that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in November of 1990, there were elections in which the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina took part, obtaining a little under 20 per cent of the seats, and then joining a coalition of the three parties, each nationalistic, one representing Serbs, one Croats, one Muslims, presided over by a seven-man presidency with Izetbegovic at its head. As early as those elections, the defendant Kordic, who had previously been active in the Communist Party, was described as a leading figure in the Busovaca municipality. In March of 1991, Tudjman and Milosevic met to discuss the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia, with little left for the Muslims. On the 25th of June of 1991, the Croatian legislature voted overwhelmingly for independence, as did a number of the constituent states of the former Yugoslavia, Slovenia. On the 21st of July of 1991, there was a meeting in Busovaca chaired by the first defendant, and if the Court would go in the supporting documents to, I think it's actually the very first page, I will draw your attention to just a few features of this first meeting. The page numbering system that I propose to use for the purpose of opening is to use the page numbers put on by the registry. They are, of course, in reverse order, for a reason I have not quite fathomed, but they start in our bundle at page 5818 at the top, and it is to those numbers that I shall be referring. This meeting, we can see two-thirds of the way down page 5818, was presided over by Dario Kordic, and over at page 5817, there is reference in paragraph 4 to the then president of the party, a man called Stjepan Kljujic, of whom you will hear more. Stjepan Kljujic was a man concerned to maintain integration of all parties within Bosnia. He was, by the terms of our days, a moderate. He wasn't to last very long in his role as president of this party. You will see comments about him in paragraphs 4 and 5. Over the page at 5816, paragraphs 17 and 18, the meeting agreed to urge Croatian population, paragraph 17, in the Travnik and Herzegovinian municipalities, to join the Croatian regional union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in order to protect Croatian interests, it is set out, that an initiative had been launched on the part of the Travnik region to establish the Croatian National Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina because of the paralysis in the performance by the BiH official authorities. At 5815, it went on to say: "The Croatian National Council will perform a function of authority in the interests of Croatian people in a given area." The document is signed by two men, Kostroman, the administrative secretary, and Dario Kordic as the chairman. From that document, if the Court would turn over to page 3 of the chronology, on the 30th of July of 1991, the first defendant was appointed coordinator of the Travnik regional community of the party. Summarised, he was already a young man, and like everybody else of this party, a recent member of the party; he was chairing effectively half of the area for the party with which you are concerned, it would appear. I make this point by way of a general observation: How is it that people younger than might be expected achieve high office in organisations? Sometimes it is because they are truly brilliant. Sometimes it is because, by being in at the ground floor, you can get on the escalator earlier. Sometimes it is because you are patronised and championed by someone of importance. All those issues may fall for determination by this Chamber in due course. On the 13th of August of 1991, at page 5811 in your papers, and in the course of a meeting held in Busovaca of the regional party, the Travnik regional party, you will see that -- I beg your pardon, page 5810 -- you will see in paragraph 3 that the behaviour of Stjepan Kljujic, the president, in relation to matters that had happened earlier, was judged unbefitting and unacceptable. He skillfully managed to avoid discussion on the decisions of the Travnik regional community. He was called on to explain his behaviour. If you will be good enough to turn over to 5508, remembering, of course, that all that is going on is going on against the background of warfare elsewhere, generated, it may be, by the Serbs. Paragraph 12: "Every municipality board must organise itself for defence, and in doing so, coordinate its activities with the unified defence system of the Croatian nation." The chairpersons for this meeting were Mate Boban, a man called Udovicic, and the defendant Kordic who was Boban's cousin and to whom he was close. Back, please, to the chronology, and over to page 4. On the 8th of October of 1991, the joint presidency of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a crisis staff committee of the party met. Page 5782 of your papers refers, and again I think we shall start at -- yes, 5782, if we look at paragraph 4, we can see the unfolding intentions of the party. "The Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall continue to advocate an independent and indivisible Bosnia and Herzegovina if that is possible, but in the event of the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina our RECOMMENDATION to the leaders of the Muslim people is after the secession of the so-called Serbian territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Muslims remain together with the Croats territorially, and that we link our territories with the Republics of Croatia and Slovenia confederally or by treaty." Over the page, paragraph 6: "As regards the policies of the SDA and the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina are INSTRUCTED not to contribute in any way to strains in relations with the Muslims; however, they should know that the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina is developing its own policies and activities independently. "Where circumstances allow, a defence system should be developed jointly with the SDA, but even in those environments it is essential to develop contingency plans for the independent defence system of the Croatian people and its territories." This document, 5779, reveals, signed by Kostroman and by Stjepan Kljujic. On the 4th of November, at your page 5773, is the record of a meeting of the Travnik regional community, presided over, and the note's signed by, Dario Kordic, as the regional community's president. At page 5773, we see this: (1) It was stated that Stjepan Kljujic, President of (the party), was not present, although he had been duly and timely invited to the meeting. (2) Conclusion --" And then there's reference to a document that I cannot lay before you. "... sent to Dr. Franjo Tudjman, was unanimously supported. Members of the Croatian Regional Community of Travnik promised to respect the secrecy of this information." There will, in due course, be evidence before this Tribunal of the regular contacts that there were between those in this part of Bosnia and Zagreb, including contacts by the first defendant himself. At page 5767, there is a letter sent to Mr. Kljujic by Dario Kordic, and it reads: "Following our telephone conversation of 5 November ... when I was put through to you by General Secretary Ivan MARKESIC, and when you told me in a thirty-second speech and I quote 'KORDIC, if you do not appear in my office tomorrow at 8 o'clock, you will be brought in by the police' --" I am sorry to the interpreters for speaking too fast. "-- I am sending you the following response: By the time you receive this fax, you will probably be familiar with the written conclusions reached at the meeting of the Travnik Regional Community held in Busovaca on 4 November, fully supporting all the clear and unambiguous positions of the Travnik Regional Community. "As we no longer live in a time of uniformity of view and blind obedience, I feel compelled to remind you that your position as President in the BH HDZ implicitly carries the obligation of living and acting among the party membership and respecting the wish of the responsible representatives of the Croats of this area that you finally attend at least one meeting of the Travnik Regional Community. I wish to inform you that the most responsible Croatian representatives of the municipalities of the Travnik Regional Community have not given me the authority to speak with you personally and particularly not tete-a-tete about the fate of our people, but if you persist with inappropriate threats and ultimatums on a meeting, it may take place, but only with all the leaders of the Travnik Regional Community in Busovaca." Signed by Mr. Kordic and sent to all representatives of the HDZ Travnik Regional Community. In due course, the Tribunal may have to decide whether what was soon to happen so far as Mr. Kljujic was concerned reflected his own shortcomings or was the result of his being a moderate and there being those who wished to supplant him and replace him. On the 12th of November of 1991, at Grude, there was a meeting of the Travnik Regional Community. The following pages in your core documents reveal the record or the conclusions, starting at 5765. I think perhaps, in accordance with the hint from the Court and indeed with my own inclinations, this is a document that should go on the ELMO because I am going to read it effectively in full, and if arrangements can be made for that to happen, I would be grateful. Your Honour, if we have, in any way, failed in our duties to the staff of your court in preparation of documents, matters of that sort, I can only apologise and say that we are, of course, feeling our way as practitioners within this room. This is, of course, an English translation. It reads as follows, in the middle of the page: "On 12 November 1991 in Grude, a working meeting was held of the presidents of the crisis staffs of the Herzegovina Regional Community and the presidents and representatives of the crisis staffs of the Travnik Regional Community." That is probably the two halves overall of this body with which we may be concerned. "The meeting was chaired by Mr. Mate Boban, Vice-President of the (party) for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Vice-President of the HDZ Crisis Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Co-chair was Mr. Dario Kordic, Co-ordinator of the Travnik Regional Community. After a several hour discussion and analysis of the political and security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and the former Yugoslavia, the participants reached the following conclusions: 1. The Herzegovina Regional Community and the Travnik Regional Community reaffirm the conclusions reached at their respective separate sessions that the Croatian people of these regions and in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina continue to support the unanimously approved declarations and conclusions adopted in the agreements with President Dr. Franjo Tudjman on 13 and 20 June 1991 in Zagreb. On the basis of the conclusions of the above-mentioned meetings and agreements in Zagreb, the separate conclusions --" And they're listed." " -- and unanimously adopt the decision that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally institute a decisive and active policy in order to bring about our age-old dream - a common Croatian State. "In order for this historical goal to become our reality in the near future, the two regional communities call for the formulation and declaration of legal and political documents (the proclamation of a Croatian banovina/entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the organisation of a referendum to join the Republic of Croatia ...) as the initial phase leading towards the final solution of the Croatian question and the creation of a sovereign Croatia within its ethnic and historical (currently possible) borders." As we turn to the second page, the Court will immediately see why I reminded you of the state of affairs between 1939 and 1941 when the Banovina existed. On the second page, paragraph 2: "2. Forces opposed to the historical interests of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina still exist within the leadership of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina. These forces advocate a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina which does not exist and in which Croatian people would be condemned to a genocide and to disappearance from the history. For that reason, the two regions are calling for decisive action which our people expect and for which they wholeheartedly embraced the HDZ. The representatives of these municipalities believe that continued waiting in silence would weaken our positions both among our own people and at the international level. We must show to Europe and to the world which territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina are Croatian and where our future lies. Under no conditions shall these people accept any other solution except the one within the borders of a free Croatia. 3. In order to implement the conclusions contained in the first two points of these Conclusions, we must: (a) Clearly define the HDZ party policy in Bosnia and Herzegovina, strengthen our membership, and select the individuals able to complete these tasks. (b) Initiate the political and legal action at the domestic and international level. (c) Make even better military preparations for a conflict with all the forces which may try to halt this inevitable process of the creation of a free Croatian State. (d) Decisively pre-empt any public or secret activity within the leadership of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina which may oppose these decisions or be damaging to them in any way." Then it is signed. The Court may conclude that the reference to "forces opposed to the historical interest" was reference to the moderates and perhaps to Mr. Kljujic; the Court may note now or later that in this particular document, there is no reference to the Serbs as the particular enemy nor any particular reference to the Muslims and to the needs for co-existence. The Court may also think that in (a), (b), (c), and (d), the document sets out in large measure what was, in due course, to happen, and the creation of the appropriate bodies and in military preparation. Not long after that, on the 18th of November of 1991, a body was created to take things further. The meeting was at Grude, and you can see reference to it at page 5757. What happened was that a community was established, at this stage described as a community, and known as Herceg-Bosna. You can see that at the top of page 5757: "on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Article 1 is, on this copy, I'm afraid, partly illegible, but Article 2 explains that "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be composed of," and then it lists a number of municipalities. Included in them Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Kiseljak, but also Vares, and going down to the south, Mostar and other places. Article 3 says that "Mostar shall be the seat of (this Community)." Article 5 says that "The Community shall respect the democratically elected government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as Bosnia-Herzegovina remains an independent state in relation to the former or any future Yugoslavia." Article 7 says that "The supreme authority of the Community shall be the Presidency, comprising the most senior representatives of the Croatian people in the municipal authority or presidents of the Croatian Democratic Union municipal boards. "The presidency shall elect the president, two deputy presidents and the secretary." So the Community of Herceg-Bosna, a quasi-state maybe, is formed, and it may well be that at this meeting you will hear evidence of a representative coming from Croatia itself to participate. We go over in the chronology of events to page 6. We have now passed through 1991 with the development of the party, with the rise of Mr. Kordic in that party, with dissatisfaction with the moderate leader of the party, and now with the establishment of this new freestanding community. On page 6 -- Your Honour, just give me one minute -- before we come to page 6, let me say this: At the end of 1991, we mark the beginning of the period covered by this indictment in specific counts, and so something of a stock-take, beyond that which I have already given you, is appropriate. Judging by the pre-trial beliefs served by the Defence, amongst the issues that you want to have in mind from this point forward include, in relation to the first defendant, Kordic, whether he, as we will see he was to become, vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, was within or outside the chain of command of the military that was in due course to be developed, the HVO. We will come to that shortly. You will be concerned with the extent of his true factual military role and power. For whatever the constitutional position, the reality is that he was often to be found in uniform and, as we shall see, often making decisions of a military nature. As the other half of that, was he only concerned with matters of logistics, administration, or being a spokesman? So far as the second defendant, Mario Cerkez, is concerned, was he, when appointed, a commander for the Vitez area generally, or was he just in charge of a small unit within it? Page 6, then, of the chronology, takes us over the turn of the year, with President Tudjman's press conference emphasising the need to solve the problem of Croatia in the way the Banovina was solved. Then in Busovaca, on the day following the recognition of Croatia by the European states, the European Community, there was a celebration at the cultural club where Kordic and Kostroman both made speeches. If our preparations have been proper, it should now be possible to play you at least part of the video that was made, a hand-held video, an amateur video, of that meeting. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This splendid and magnificent rally was worth shedding litres of blood and sweat for, to experience this dream finally which, for nine centuries, was just a dream for the Croatian people: An independent sovereign -- inaudible -- tens of thousands and -- state of Croatia. If last night we feared perhaps that there would be no marking or celebrating here in Busovaca, many were deceived. The Croatian spirit lives here in Busovaca. This evening is proof that the Croatian people in Busovaca is also part of the united Croatian nation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am happy to stop the tape there for this reason. The Court will in due course hear the tape in full. It will then have the advantage of a full transcript of what was said and will be able to consider it at greater leisure. I don't believe you have a transcript within your papers, and can I just tell you one or two of the things that were said and make a couple of points about this meeting. First, in the passage that I think preceded where the interpreters picked up this morning, and that's no doubt my fault in not getting things properly teed up, there are certainly two references in the speeches by the first defendant to the independent state of Croatia, which was indeed the name of the state that existed between 1941 and 1945. There was reference, as you can see, to the magnificent rally, how it was worth shedding litres of blood and sweat for the dream of centuries to become true. There was further reference of gratitude to the German nation and to the German state, which will have to be interpreted; of course, Germany had been or may have been the first country to recognise the position of this party and of the independence of Bosnia. But in the second speech, which we didn't show any part of but which you will see in due course, where Kostroman was speaking, he made this point. He said: "As for the remaining population in our areas, the question asked is, "What about the Muslims, what about the Serbs and everyone else?" We can say to them, let them not worry about anything, let them live in our state of Croatia and no one will miss even a hair on their heads if they accept us as their brothers and accept the fact that they will be citizens of the state of Croatia." There were indeed Muslims present in the hall on this occasion in Busovaca, although the audience of Croats was drawn more widely than just from that town. Even those who were not present soon got to learn of it as an event, and indeed the videotape that we've just seen in part was seen by others, and to them it was an alarming display, unsettling, creating fear, and forecasting, the Court may ultimately decide, exactly what was to come. If we can return, please, to the chronology. Without troubling you with the documents themselves, on the 25th of January, there was an apparent resignation by the first defendant from his position as deputy president of the newly formed body of Herceg-Bosna to which he had apparently been appointed. His resignation was expressed to be by reason of the fact that representatives of the people weren't making enough effort, and so on. The letter was addressed to Boban. But it seems not to have been effective, and indeed was rejected on the 27th of January; and whether it was a real and genuine resignation or whether it was all part of an overall aim at reaching more power and authority will be for the Tribunal to decide. It was rejected, and on the 29th of January of 1992, page 5733 in your papers, and as part of a decision made on the 29th of January at Grude, we see the developing power of the institutions that had been created. Just to remind ourselves, first the party, then the community of Herceg-Bosna, and at page 5733, at the foot of the page, heading "Re-examination of Staff Appointments." "The competent bodies of the HDZ of BH are to immediately collect written approvals from the HDZ municipal boards responsible for all staff on a local level appointed to represent the HDZ of BH. Those who do not receive the approval must immediately have dismissal procedures initiated against them, while the appointment of new staff should proceed according to the regulated procedure. A candidate who is not a member of the party cannot be appointed to a post in the bodies of the Republic." So the party was strengthening its grip. Over the page, please, to page 7 of the chronology. On the 28th of February of 1992, we have either the first or an early record of Mr. Kordic's involvement in apparently military matters. On this occasion, a report from the European monitors dealing with a roadblock that then existed in Donja Puticevo, recorded dealing with the first defendant and there being present a large number of uniformed men in Croatian camouflage uniforms with Croatian cap symbols and arm badges with "HOS," a unit operating in that area, clearly marked. Shortly after this, and following a referendum, on the 6th of March, Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence, and that was ultimately recognised by Europe and the United States. And there is then a record from a newspaper on the 6th of March of somebody, a man called Skravan, recording that he had been told by Kordic and a man called Stipac that they were working to create a Croatian republic and that Kordic had showed the areas of the parastate, or that the parastate was to seize, if necessary, by force of arms. Mr. Kordic of course is shown as having no military training of any kind, but over the page, at page 8, on the 9th of March, he was identified as a colonel in the report of a press conference. On the 15th of March, Kljujic, the moderate, was ousted, the formal completion of his being ousted being revealed a little later. On the 17th of March there was a decision made at a meeting of leaders of the municipal boards of Zenica, Busovaca, Vitez, and Travnik that as a municipality bordering on the municipalities of Herceg-Bosna, Zenica was now also to be included in its defence system. So the community was becoming larger. On the 21st of March -- this deals with what true role the defendant Kordic had -- bears the record and indeed the paper showing a request to the Ministry of Defence of Croatia for a meeting between various parties to be attended by, amongst others, the first defendant. So was he just dealing with publicity and matters of logistics, or was he fully active in all affairs of the developing Herceg-Bosna? At the foot of this page, on the 7th of April, when Croatia recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state, it offered all Bosnian Croats dual nationality. That may have had at least two effects. It may more likely have secured the position of President Tudjman if, as he judged, these would be voters sympathetic to his cause; and of course it may have encouraged whatever ambitions there lay in the hearts of Croatian residents within Bosnia and Herzegovina to be linked to the Croatia state itself. On the 8th of April of 1992, the presidency of that parastate or quasi-state, Herceg-Bosna, set up the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, as the supreme defence body of Herceg-Bosna. If we go over to page 9 of the chronology, the order signed by Mate Boban stated that it was the only legal body with command over defence forces; that the HVO main staff will communicate only with municipal HVO staffs; and that all other military formations in HZ-HB are either illegal or hostile, and other names will be removed from official use, so that within this community established by the party, there is now a body having a near monopoly, or a monopoly, of power and control. Three entries further down, you'll see the first reference to the second defendant, Mario Cerkez. His entries on this schedule remain identified by the use of italic script. A crisis committee in the spring of 1992, evidence will reveal, was created, and Cerkez was one of the members of that, along with five Muslims, and it held meetings during which he was a participant. On the 3rd of May of 1992, in Busovaca, we will see that there were orders signed by Kordic, this one in particular, and I needn't take you to it. It is significant perhaps only because he signed over an HVO stamp. If the issue is that he was never a member of the HVO and had no real function in the HVO, why, amongst other things, was he signing documents in the ways he was to sign them -- and we'll see many of them -- and why here was he signing over an HVO stamp? In early May he was seen by witnesses, or one, certainly, dressed in HVO uniform. Later, three entries up from the bottom of this page, with many soldiers, HVO soldiers, he visited the factory in Novi Travnik in order to enforce his request for some rocket launchers. Dressed in uniform at the time, he secured his desire, and the launcher was driven off in the general direction of Gornji Vakuf. Similarly, last entry on this page, in the Travnik Technical Maintenance Institute, he was found visiting with HVO troops, requesting equipment for the HVO, dressed in uniform, or at any event wearing the HVO insignia. These developments in Busovaca associated with rising concern amongst the Muslims, soon to face a significant change in the order of their lives. At page 10 of the chronology, and at page 5688 of your documents, on the 10th of May, apparently from Busovaca, an order was pronounced, signed, as we can see, on the following page, 5687, by Dario Kordic as HVO vice-president and another person as commander of the municipal HVO. An order was signed of 18 paragraphs which may have become imprinted on the minds of Muslim residents. At paragraph 1, it said that, "The agreement between the HVO and the so-called Busovaca TO on the distribution of weapons is hereby terminated ..." There had, until this stage, been some agreement between Croats and Muslims, who of course for long enough had been fighting a common foe and fighting together; it's one of the complexities of this whole history, of which no doubt this Tribunal is in part or substantially aware, they had been fighting collectively, and there had been agreements about the sharing of weapons. In any event, that agreement was terminated. "... it has been decided that the Busovaca HVO forces take over all weapons, equipment, material, as well as the barracks. "2. The town of Busovaca is to be completely blocked from all sides. "3. All paramilitary formations (the so-called TO), individuals and others are given the ultimatum to hand over all weapons in their possession by Sunday 1200 hrs, or to place themselves under HVO command, which includes the wearing of HVO insignia. "4. Until all previously set conditions are fulfilled, no HVO representative has the right to negotiate with representatives of the so-called TO and the Patriotic League." "5. A warrant of arrest is issued," and three names are given. Prominent Muslims were arrested, two of them, I think, just for a day or so; one of them for rather longer, and not leaving without injury as a result of beatings. Over the page. "7. The mobilisation of all Busovaca HVO forces is to be completed." 10, a curfew. 15 and onwards. "The PTT building is to be taken over and used by the HVO." Indeed, that became the first defendant's base. He had premises there in the basement. "16. Weapons and HVO uniforms shall be seized from combatants who refuse to consistently carry out the order in any way. "17. Protection of vital town facilities and houses belonging to the families of the HVO leaders is to be reinforced. "18. This order is to be handed to the commander of the nonexistent TO of Busovaca ... by a messenger. The receipt of the order is to be signed." This order, the ultimatum to hand over weapons, the arresting of leading Muslims and their detention, constituted a take-over of the town of Busovaca. From that time and until the end of the year of 1992, residents of that town, from whom you will hear, had to live with that reality and the limitations it imposed on them. On the 19th of May, page 5686 in your documents, please, we see further examples of the authority which now existed in the first defendant. On the 19th of May, he was giving a movement permit to somebody to move across the territory of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Croatia. He was being permitted to carry weapons, and HVO checkpoints were ordered to allow him unfettered passage. Signed for the regional staff of the Central Bosnia HVO by Dario Kordic. The following page in your papers, page 5685, an order signed -- incidentally, there's an error here, I'm almost certain, because we only have the English version, but if you look at the foot of the page, it says that Dario Kordic signed as president of the Croatian Community. I think that should read "vice-president," and the word "pro," or the letters "pro," that was probably hidden under a stamp or something in the original text has been cut out. It is vice-president; there is no change there. This document, this order recalled in paragraph 1: "... the HVO forces in Busovaca are ordered to guard the important buildings of the municipal territory in the future, according to the order of the commander of the Busovaca HVO municipal command." It sets out the curfew in paragraph 2. In paragraph 3, it says this: "All workers of the governmental bodies of Busovaca Municipal Assembly, workers of all companies and institutions ... and the public security service, (except for individuals who do not wish to submit themselves to the HVO command)." And it then sets out what those people are to do. But if people do not report for work, they will lose their jobs -- that comes towards the end of that paragraph -- so that jobs were now for members of the HVO. You will be hearing from witnesses of the loss of jobs, or sometimes, I think, just the diminution of status, but the loss of jobs by Muslims who were being cut out of their former life in this particular municipality. Over the page -- I see the time, and I don't know to what extent the Court is flexible; I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Neither more nor less convenient than any other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it is now clear that my estimate of concluding this morning was optimistic. Nevertheless, I hope I won't go too far into the afternoon. But I think it's an inevitability. I got us, I think, to page 5684 in the papers, which was an order for some equipment for Busovaca units. The significance of it again, that he's signing for the regional HVO staff of Central Bosnia, that on the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You dealt, in fact, with 5685.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so grateful, yes. In which case then, this would be the next one, and its simple significance is the signature at the bottom, and I can pass on quite swiftly. On page 5683, there is yet another order, again signed in a similar way, and at 5681, an order, in these terms: "The Municipal Headquarters of the HVO in Vares is hereby ordered to send a unit of 30 soldiers immediately on receipt of this order to protect the village of Tarcin Do because there is an immediate danger of the Chetniks attacking the village." The Court will have in mind that, of course, Vares is the separate community, the other side, I think, of Serb presence on the ground, and the Court will be interested, as we develop the case, to see the recurring communications between the first defendant and Vares. In any case, he signs this document again as vice-president of the HVO. We can go over to page 11 of the chronology. The next document, I think, of this type would be 5673, a similar document to something we have seen earlier, where he is signing, for the HVO Central Bosnia regional headquarters, a permanent pass in respect of someone permitted to pass and to carry weapons. On the 19th of June, according to a radio broadcast, the first defendant signed a communique announcing that the HVO was the only legal supreme commander of Herceg-Bosna and of all its residents, and at about this same time, the police station in Vitez was captured or taken over by the HVO, and as you will see in the next entry on the chronology, there was an attack on Novi Travnik, Novi Travnik northwest of the map we have been looking at and a little south of Travnik itself. What was the level of this attack? It was about an hour long. It resulted in the removal of Territorial Defence Muslim forces from various premises where they had been quartered. So that things are edging up in scale from what happened in Busovaca with the taking over of the town, with arrest of people, now perhaps one of the early attacks by Croats on Muslims or Bosniaks, as I think may sometimes be the more appropriate terminology, and I must check that with the witnesses as I call them, now an early attack. At the foot of page 11 of the chronology, again, the first defendant signing himself as deputy president for the HVO along with Kostroman. Kostroman was the secretary of the party. He is the man who I referred to speaking after Kordic on the hand-held video, and you will see that in detail in due course. But as deputy president, he ordered the HVO in Vares temporarily to accommodate HVO from another unit, and that can be found on page 5670 of your documents, another short document. The Croatian Defence Council in Vares municipality was ordered to allow uninterrupted activity to the Croatian Defence Council of the Ilijas municipality in Vares since they can't work in the Ilijas municipality. Was this man really no member of the HVO? Was he a man who had no authority over its affairs? If you please, to page 12 of the chronology, we must pick up a little now of what was happening so far as the second defendant is concerned, bearing in mind what may be being asserted in due course about his extremely limited role. In the summer, he was seen briefing soldiers before the taking of a storage depot and briefing soldiers before the action to repulse Serbs in an area north of Turbe. He was also participating in an oath-taking ceremony at the stadium in Vitez under the presidency of the first defendant where HVO soldiers made an oath to defend everything that was Croatian. In a newspaper in July of 1992, the first defendant was quoted as saying: "We want one-third of the State's power and no one is going to give us anything. We just want to take what is ours." On the 3rd of July, several decrees were published. One of them is set out quite extensively here, and I will just read an important part of it, for it identifies one of the issues with which you will be having to deal. It is the presidency of Herceg-Bosna decreeing various matters, and if you pass your eyes down to halfway down the entry, and indeed about halfway down the page, Article 29, dealing with command and control of the armed forces, stated, amongst other things, "that the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna is the President of Herceg-Bosna who shall determine ..." And then within a subparagraph, subparagraph 7, that he should appoint and relieve of duty military commanders in accordance with a respective legal act. The supreme commander is the president of the community, not the vice-president, Dario Kordic. He is a member of the presidency, and it's asserted, it may be, that commanding the armed forces being within the office of the president, that the vice-president, or any one of them, is outside that chain of command. Well, there are two answers to that. First of all, there is what was actually happening on the ground. The second is that there was a further decision on the same day, which I'm afraid I haven't got in your papers, and that can be remedied in due course, but it was the statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration in the territory of Herceg-Bosna which did repose, it will be argued and may so be decided, authority over the HVO in the presidency. So that is an issue that you will have before you to resolve on evidence in due course. If we turn over in the chronology to page 13, the latter part of July of 1992, the first entry marked the 12th of July, I wonder if everyone could be good enough simply to delete it? It's a rogue entry; it shouldn't be there. It was the 12th of August and it never was the 12th of July, and it has already been entered as the 12th of August. On the 16th of July, a couple of entries further down, there will be a document -- it's not in your papers at the moment -- of Cerkez signing the military identification of someone, identifying him as a member of the 1st Brigade in Vitez. The Court will remember -- it's got in mind perhaps as an issue generally: What was the second defendant's authority in Vitez? Was it a small and single brigade, or was it the general authority for that area? In August of 1992, there was a speech made by the first defendant about the restructuring of the HVO units and his asserting that Novi Travnik would soon be Croatian. Novi Travnik, an area they plainly wanted to command. They maybe never succeeded, but it was the subject of recurring attempts. They wanted it for Croatia or for themselves, the Croats. In the schedule as it is presently constituted, I have not identified all the attacks on various locations. Some are identified; some are not. Various reasons for that, one of which is that sometimes dating of the attacks is more difficult to be precise about than one might think, and it is perhaps better to await the evidence. However, on the 8th of September, there is an attack in the region by the HVO, referred to in the amended indictment, not the subject of a count in the indictment, but it's interesting to see what level of violence was being used by one community on the other at this stage because it is a developing pattern. The village concerned was Potkraj and Duhri, that's P-O-T-K-R-A-J, and Duhri, D-U-H-R-I, and on or about the 8th of August, there was an attack by the HVO on this village, which is towards the southeast of the area with which we are concerned, near to Kiseljak, and it was initially with small arms and later with heavier weapons, and as a result of the attack on that day, one Muslim civilian was killed in Duhri and one in the other village of Potkraj. A Croat civilian was also killed. That is, of course, a terrible event. Any death is a terrible event, however it occurs. But for the purposes of this case, maybe of even greater evidential significance is that 28 houses were burned down. So that one can see the developing pattern of behaviour leading to control or, of course, to the expulsion of one community from the territory aspired to by the other. Back to the chronology, and without troubling you to go to the papers on this occasion, on the 12th of August, the first defendant, signing this time in his role as vice-president of the community, Herceg-Bosna, an invitation to the HVO president in Vares to attend a meeting in Busovaca. Over the page, and I can deal with these entries quite shortly, just to identify their type. On the 31st of August, as vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, signing approval for the free movement of people. On the 2nd of September, there is a handwritten note by somebody called Ivica Rajic, instructing the Vares party official that the first defendant was a person to ask for additional money for troops. On the 7th of September, the first defendant, in his position as vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, signing or co-signing a request or instruction to municipal headquarters for platoons to be sent to Jajce the same day, co-signed by Blaskic in his capacity as commander of Central Bosnia. Incidentally, I said earlier this morning that the defendant, the first defendant, had no military training. That, of course, reflects different regimes in different countries. There was, of course, I suspect, compulsory military training for him with the JNA at that time. That says nothing about his being officer rank or how he could achieve so quickly the rank of colonel. Over to page 15 of the schedule. On the 18th of September, the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself dealt with the decrees that established the Community of Herceg-Bosna, the internal community, and annulled them as not lawful. Incidentally, Herceg-Bosna has never been, was never, recognised internationally at all. The 19th of September of 1992 is an order by Blaskic in which the handling and transportation of weapons was to be dealt with or was being dealt with in order that they should move through checkpoints on their way to Herzegovina, the southern part of the area in which we have a general interest, or on to Croatia from Central Bosnia. The order said weapons and ammunition must be accompanied by papers signed by both Blaskic and the first defendant Dario Kordic. On the 19th of September -- we turn again to the second defendant just to see what's developing there. It's page 5610 in your papers. If the Court has found that page ... On this day, the 19th of September, the second defendant signs, as staff commander for Vitez HVO, a request to the HVO in Travnik: "Because of the formation of special forces in Vitez HVO, we hereby ask for you to issue us as many beds, mattresses and blankets as possible. "The special units will be quartered in the barracks, which we have prepared for the further functioning and training of special forces. "GOD AND CROATS." And then he signs. On page 5608 is the beginning of a long document dated the 22nd of September from Busovaca. I am wondering if this is one -- again, I am going to be jumping through it, I'm afraid, so quickly that -- no, perhaps we ought to put another one on the ELMO, it is only right, if we can dig it all out, it's several pages. 5608. While the usher is helping us, this is, on its face, an excerpt from the minutes of the meeting of the Croatian Defence Council in municipalities of Central Bosnia. That's page 1. Thank you very much. It's attended by, amongst others, Dario Kordic, and we see that the working presidency is described as Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, Tihomir Blaskic, and Ignac Kostroman. There is a report on the situation in the municipalities, and if we could go to the fourth sheet, please, to our page 5605, not forgetting the other comparative outpost of the area with which we are concerned, Zepce, in the far north or the north of the small area -- not the far north -- there is a report here on Zepce: "Civilian HVO authority has not been established. Military HVO authority is in operation for the municipalities of Zepce ..." And others are named. "These municipalities recently officially joined the HZ-HB. Muslims have reacted strongly and there is a possibility of an armed confrontation. The military command does not have professional staff, so that it will be difficult to protect these areas without significant staff changes. The town is poorly supplied ... Muslims do not want to go to the front lines." At the foot of that page begins -- right at the foot of that page, please, just the last two lines, thank you, and over to the next page -- "Travnik": "Until now there has been a kind of dual authority which was at variance with the army. Military command is separate. Muslims are trying to take over all civilian and military authority in the city. Until recently there were five kinds of police station. There are many mujahedins in the city. The HVO government has recently been detaching itself from the joint municipal government. It has also been planning the Central Bosnia Chief HVO Command to move to Travnik. Certain out-posted ministerial departments for Central Bosnia would be moved from Mostar to Travnik. The following are also moving to Travnik: Vice-President of the HZ-HB, Ante Valenta; Vice-President of the HZ-HB, Dario Kordic; and the Chief Secretary of the HZ-HB, Ignac Kostroman." In that line, we identify two of the names that I probably should have identified by title earlier, the other vice-president and the secretary that I referred to a little earlier. "It is also possible that the HVO Chief of Staff of Central Bosnia with the commander, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, will also move to Travnik. The reasons these offices are moving to Travnik is to make Travnik a political Croatian centre for Central Bosnia. There are presently about 16.000, mostly Muslim, refugees in Travnik. It is estimated that about 80.000, mostly Muslim, refugees have passed from Krajina through Travnik. The town is well supplied, considering the war conditions." There is also a report at this document, at the foot of this page, on that northeastern outpost, Vares. This is the most protruding municipality of the HB. "The economy has practically ground to a halt. People are almost starving. The HVO is in full control. About 82.000 refugees have passed through from the direction of Brcko and Tuzla." Next page, "Transit taxes are collected. It will not be possible to apply tax rates as prescribed in the HZ-HB decree. Schools have started working in the Croatian language. The town is poorly supplied. Vares received some aid from the commodity reserves, but that was very little. There are about 1200 Muslim and 800 Croatian refugees. Refugee camps are being built." In the middle of this page, perhaps worth noting, under the heading "Observations noted in all the Municipalities," this was the expressed view. "In almost all the municipalities, Muslims are behaving as if they have an exclusive right to power in B and H and as if they are the only fighters for B and H; "All permits must be urgently made uniform and instructions issued as to jurisdiction; "There has to be strong HVO propaganda everywhere; "Muslims have attempted to enforce their policy through the HOS," that's the Croatian Defence force, "but have been discovered. In Central Bosnia, the HOS have almost completely put themselves under the command of the HVO. In many areas, the HOS has been dissolved and its members have joined the HVO." Then the last page of this document, our page 5601, and indeed the penultimate paragraph: "HVO Military bodies for Central Bosnia shall prepare defence plans against possible attack by Islamic Fundamentalist Mujahedin Forces and introduce military discipline and order in the military formations." Then, "The Ministry of Defence shall, together with the military command, provide military logistics for Central Bosnia." The signatures to this document being the two deputy presidents and the secretary. We now -- thank you very much; that's what I wanted, that document. Yes. If the Court would turn in the immediate following document, which starts at page 5600, it will find a "Situation At The Novi Travnik Front" report that I'm only concerned at this stage to go two pages on, to 5598, paragraph 10, bearing in mind the issue about the first defendant's involvement in military matters. This document, signed by both Blaskic and the first defendant, has as paragraph 10: "While defence operations are being conducted, the vice-president of the HZ-HB /Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna/ Dario Kordic and I are in Novi Travnik, continuously leading the military operations with deep knowledge of the situation and by keeping all the forces under control. Commander of" -- and then there's a problem with the original document -- reference to "Filip Filipovic is also here and the Novi Travnik HVO HQ." So another document which the Prosecution say fits, and only fits, with this man having by now assumed considerable responsibility in matters military and with consent of all those others involved at the senior level of the party of the HVO. If in the chronology we can now turn to page 16, in the autumn of 1992, on the 19th of October, there was an incident where the first defendant demanded that the barricade that had been set up by Bosniaks at Ahmici should be removed. Ahmici lies beside the road running south and east and is plainly a critical point on that road. He stated that there would be no negotiations until there had been surrender to the HVO at that point. On the same day, the second defendant made contact with the first defendant in relation to this same topic, the first defendant saying that the checkpoint had to be removed or he would not be responsible for what happened. There was, I think, an effort or a successful effort at enforced removal of the barricades from a Catholic cemetery at Ahmici, a little further down, apparently directly on the orders of the first defendant. At the same time, what's the position with the second defendant? Simon Ellis met him at the Vitez Hotel, and he was introduced to that witness as the local military man in charge of the HVO. Over to page 17 in the chronology, on the 20th of October, with the continuing problems at the Ahmici roadblock or checkpoint, the first defendant overheard saying what would happen to those Muslims if the barricades weren't lifted. In this opening, I'm not concerned to forecast in detail some of the more potentially, as it were, exciting or excitable bits of evidence, for several reasons. One, this opening is basically to set the Prosecution's case and to assist the Court and to point it to where the evidence will be coming from; second, because although there is evidence from time to time of absolutely direct involvement by one defendant and the other in criminal matters, it's not evidence upon which we are dependent for establishing our case, as we have made plain in our pre-trial brief; third, because in the nature of things, forecasts of evidence are sometimes not realised or not fully realised. But I point the Court to the possibility or probability that there will be evidence of a direct kind at about this point in the trial. On that same day, Colonel Stewart of the British Battalion had to deal with organising a cease-fire for the problem that was then involving fighting, and what was significant or what may have been significant is that the first defendant was able to set out the terms of a cease-fire agreement without seeking authority from anyone else. He appeared, it may be, to have been his own master. The next four entries relate to an attack at Travnik. They relate to Cerkez. Again there is the potential for direct evidence of what he said and how that would impact on those at the receiving end of the attack by the HVO. For the same reason, I leave it there. On the 21st of October of 1992, and at page 5600 in -- it may be an incorrect reference -- it's a wrong reference, in which case I shan't take your time with it. Don't worry about -- I'll move on without taking you to the document, but on that day, the first defendant signed, together with Blaskic, a report on the situation in Novi Travnik. No, I've already taken you to it; we've already looked at it. I'm so sorry. It's slightly out of order. Yes, we've already dealt with it. We can go over now to page 18, the latter part of October of 1992. The first entry reveals how, at a time when there were attacks being mounted in Novi Travnik and outside the immediate area, but in Mostar and Prozor, Mostar having been taken by the Croats and declared to be the capital of Herceg-Bosna, while those actions were taking place, there is evidence of Kordic and Blaskic issuing an order for the shelling of Bugojno on certain terms. As to Novi Travnik, we have heard what happened to it in its short suffering earlier in June. In October, the level of the attack was more sustained and may have involved Kordic personally. The result of the attack was to consolidate certainly control by the HVO of parts of that municipality, and it involved the destruction of many Muslim-owned businesses located in the area that did fall to the HVO. At the same time, if we keep an eye on approximate dates, as the third entry on this particular page, Cerkez features having a meeting with a witness to be called, inviting him to negotiate on an issue, a defence issue relating to roadblocks in that area. In the middle of the page, on television, the first defendant recorded as saying what would happen to Ahmici in the event of and as a result of the blocking of the movement of troops going to Novi Travnik. Further down this page, and in your papers at page 5582, a document signed by Blaskic on the 10th of November dealing with talks that were to take place or expected to take place with General Morillon and an invitation that had been issued for a meeting with top-level HVO politicians as soon as possible. Paragraph 2, the Serbian proposal is set out as to where the talks should take place, the representative of the Serbian side is identified, and at paragraph 4, "Subject of talk, immediate cease-fire in Mostar. I propose that our side is represented by deputy president of the HZ-HB," that's the Herceg-Bosna Community, "Mr. Dario Kordic, and secretary Ignac Kostroman." And that was to be reflected in due course by some of the things in which the first defendant participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While it's in my mind, let me ask you this, Mr. Nice, since it may occur to others: The first accused is the vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Reference is made to "the president" throughout these documents and in what you say. What is the Prosecution case about his role?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Prosecution -- this is a man reported as dead, the president himself, so that the Prosecution hasn't in any formal way, I think, expressed its view, but its view, of course, is that responsibility would also lie there in almost all circumstances, but that that case has not been explored or developed because it hasn't been possible to focus on him because he has been reported as dead. On the chronology -- can I make another point while I've interrupted the -- broken into the narrative. I don't intend to go through the indictment in any detail in the course of this opening, because they are very long documents, and they have been considered by the Court and by my friends for the Defence and so on. But it's probably worth reminding the Court or informing the Court that the way the indictment is formulated is that there is first of all the persecution count, which encompasses pretty nearly everything, or everything, followed by specific counts dealing with killings and attacks and inhuman treatment and matters of that sort. Generally, the indictment is confined in the case of Cerkez, of course, to the immediate area of his concern; so far as Kordic is concerned, for most matters, that is for particular offences, to the particular Opstinas we have looked at on that map. So far as persecution is concerned, because of his role within the HVO generally, he is also indicted for what happened in the area of Herceg-Bosna generally, i.e. all the way down to Mostar, so that when we see references to what's happening in Mostar, its relevance, direct relevance, can be in that respect. At the foot of page 18 of the chronology, we see that there was in Mostar the second general assembly meeting of the party with a number of Croatian guests, with the first defendant being present, with rules of procedure being adopted, and so on, and then over to the top of page 19, Mate Boban elected president and Kordic elected vice-president with four others. Incidentally, I made reference to a relationship between Boban and Kordic; that's -- I should make plain, and I'm grateful for being reminded of this or informed of this -- that comes from witnesses, in the sense that the relationship of cousin might have been believed by witnesses, but it may be that it is not something that I am in a position to prove any more than that, so it's by repute on the part of some of the witnesses, and I don't put it higher than that. But now, in November of 1992, his status formally as vice-president, with others, of the party for this area. Towards the foot of page 19 of the chronology, we come to the 28th of November and page 5548 of your papers. This is one of a category of documents with which you will, if not already familiar in other cases, become familiar here, reports on the situation from observers who one might expect to be dispassionate. It says in the discussion, "Opening, General," and this is at Sarajevo airport, "All delegations were present and welcomed by the chairman. Col Kordic was the new chairman of the HVO delegation. He introduced himself as the superior of Col Blaskic and he stated that he would be in attendance at all future MMWG meetings." Then there was a meeting, and so on. At the foot of page 19 of the same page in the schedule, in a newspaper article, the first defendant is reported as having given a speech at a swearing-in ceremony for HVO soldiers of a particular brigade, referring to Zenica as Croatian space and an integral part of HZ-HB. Then over the page to page 20, in an interview published, five lines down, I think, or six lines down, one of his replies was to this effect: "It is a firm foundation of a future Croat national constitution with equal rights to the other two parties in this sovereign and internationally recognised Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." It goes on: "He said that the Croat people have never wanted any kind of ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they have never fought for cantons. Asked whether Bosnia and Herzegovina is a Croat homeland, he observed that it's mostly occupied; that to feel this to be so is the way to regain the occupied territory. To realise this aim, we have to use all methods including military, political, and the international community." Well, there is a reported assertion of no desire for other than equal rights to the other parties. Of course, there may be reasons for speaking differently to the press or the international press than in other settings, and in any event, whatever is said has to be judged not only beside other things that are said but beside what is done. In the middle of this page, on the 3rd of December, Cerkez became the deputy commander, it may be, according to a milinfosum report, the deputy commander based in Vitez.
