Even taking their case as stated, if there were such a plan, there is no evidence of it after the date of the referendum, which is before the date of 10 May, 1992, on which I propose that the Tribunal should dismiss the persecution allegation. Moving then to the predicate offences, and that is Counts 3 through 45, which are, as paragraph 37 of the amended complaint indicates and as my learned colleague has indicated, are really the heart and soul, the specific acts, the specific persecutory acts alleged and on which their persecution count is predicated, those predicate acts, in our judgment, even taking their case as stated, as if it were true -- which we do not -- taking it on that basis, we believe that they have not pointed to direct evidence of the commission, direct commission, by our client, Mr. Kordic, of those acts from Counts 3 through 45. Secondly, as to indirect liability, as an aider and abettor or in other fashion, under section 7(1), Your Honour, we would point out that under section 7(1), there has to be proof beyond a reasonable doubt of assistance by Mr. Kordic in a specific crime that contributed directly and substantially to the commission of that crime and there must be the requisite specific and deliberate intent so to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is for aiding and abetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In other words, I have made an argument that there is simply no evidence of direct commission. There is evidence that can be said to relate to, be relevant to aiding and abetting, but my argument is that there is not sufficient evidence, not nearly sufficient evidence, given the circumstantial nature of the case, to convict for aiding and abetting or any other form of indirect liability under section 7(1), and I would point you to paragraphs 22 through 25 of our volume 1 pre-trial brief where we lay out, in arguments following that, why we believe the Prosecutor's case, as stated in their papers and as stated by my learned colleague today, simply does not meet the relevant test of specific linkage in terms of assistance directly and substantially contributing to the commission of a specific predicate offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, that argument really goes to the heart of this case, doesn't it? Because what the Prosecution are inviting us to do is to draw an inference from circumstantial evidence and say that the inference to be drawn is that the accused were involved and participated in these offences. Now, at this stage, of course, it can be no more than an invitation. It is something which we have to consider and we will have to consider on the evidence. But to dismiss the case without hearing anything would be to take a fairly drastic line of action, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It would indeed, Your Honour, be to take a drastic line of action, and the Defence understands that. We urge it because we believe the weakness of the circumstantial case put on by the Prosecutor warrants it. We have explained why we believe that is true. I would urge Your Honours that in a situation in which there are alternative theories that explain an accused's conduct as innocent and lawful, on the one hand, versus illegal on the other, or where there are conflicting but plausible theories, and we have laid out a theory based on the documents that the Prosecutor has advanced in our pre-trial brief and invited the Court to consider whether there is any way, even if the case is proved, as the Prosecutor proposes to prove it, that there can be a finding beyond a reasonable doubt that the necessary assistance in the specific crime contributed directly and substantially to that crime with the requisite, specific, and deliberate intent to do so, and I am simply urging Your Honours to consider this matter at the outset, rule upon it. We believe there is simply not sufficient specificity, and that is why we raise it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Smith. I was wondering, did you not forget part of Article 7(1) because you mentioned aiding and abetting and such like but you failed to mention the first part of 7(1) which mentions planning, instigation, ordering, and that is what we call "command responsibility." Do you mean that there can be no such issue at stake here, no issue of command responsibility, in what we have heard to date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say two things in response: The first is that we believe and we urge in our briefs that planning, instigating, as opposed to direct commission under section 7(1), have essentially the same characteristics in terms of what must be proved as aiding and abetting because they are forms of indirect liability, and therefore, I thought I had addressed them. I addressed them implicitly by just dealing with aiding and abetting. I apologise if, by not mentioning the other names, I have not made myself clear to the Court. The second thing I would say, however, is that it is our strong view, and we have argued it, that section 7(1) is not a command responsibility section. That theory, if at all, and we have argued that the language doesn't accomplish it, and you have overruled us, but that argument is a section 7(3) argument, in our judgment, and a clear distinction must be made between command responsibility under section 7(3) where there is a superior-subordinate relationship. We do not believe that there is a superior-subordinate relationship shown in this case. But that theory is a section 7(3) theory and it is not a basis for imposing liability under section 7(1). Indirectly there one must deal with the law relating to the aiding and abetting, the assistance in the commission of a crime, irrespective of the command responsibility issue. So I have been trying to draw a bright line between command responsibility with a superior-subordinate relationship, which we believe is not shown under section 7(3), and the showing of assistance in a specific crime where there has to be direct and substantial assistance to the commission of that crime, specific crime, and the requisite, specific, and deliberate intent to do so. We are urging the dismissal of the indictment on the grounds that, while there is a mountain of information that is being arrayed on the question of this general theory of persecution, there is simply, when you look carefully at it, no specific evidence linking, directly or indirectly, Mr. Kordic to the specific allegations under 7(1), and there is no evidence of a superior-subordinate hierarchy and relationship that would hold him accountable to the standards applicable to, in effect, a military officer, and we have made those arguments in our briefs, Your Honour, at some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, it seems to me that you have implicitly agreed with the Presiding Judge that your motion is a bit premature. I understood you to be saying, and I put it the way it is expressed in some jurisdictions, that where you have two inferences that can be drawn, one favourable to the accused and the other the other way, then you are obliged to draw the inference favouring the accused for the simple reason that you would not have proof beyond a reasonable doubt, but you cannot ask us to do that now because we haven't heard the evidence yet, and this is why I say I think you are implicitly agreeing that your motion is premature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would respond to Your Honour by saying that we were arguing that the -- if you will just forgive me for a moment -- the argument is not premature. You can rule now on the simple question of whether, on the basis of the existing evidence, they have met, even, in effect, a prima facie threshold, and if there is not sufficient evidence, it seems to me you can dismiss, and the argument on the alternative theories I am suggesting is based on the existing evidence they have already adduced when, as the trial goes forward, we will, of course, ourselves adduce evidence on the alternative theories, and it may be that you will conclude that it is premature on the grounds that there is sufficient evidence at this time for going forward. We are simply arguing and urging you to consider whether there is sufficient evidence even to proceed on the predicate offence counts. I hope I have made myself clear and answered your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a final point, and that is whether we have any power to deal with this motion at the moment. There is a power in Rule 98 bis to enter motion for judgment and acquittal. That is after the close of the case for the Prosecution when the Trial Chamber finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction. Now, I don't know of any other Rule which would allow us, even if we were minded to at this stage, to dismiss the case, to dismiss the indictment, after the Prosecution has opened the case but before its called its evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I would rely upon your general power to issue orders and on the practice in jurisdictions, all jurisdictions I'm familiar with, to allow a testing of the Prosecutor's case at the outset. In any case, I might say that if there are concerns about whether my second motion on the predicate offences is proper at this time or whether the facts are sufficient to go forward, I would still urge Your Honours to consider the motion on persecution and whether there are persecutory acts either outside Central Bosnia or outside the time periods running from 10 May to October 23rd, 1993 -- 10 May, '92. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall dismiss these motions. All the matters which counsel raises are matters which will be dealt with or not in evidence. If the evidence does not support the counts, as the Prosecution anticipate it will, then, of course, those counts will fall. But to rule at this stage would be premature, and as I just mentioned, I doubt we have the power in this Tribunal to do it. We will adjourn now. We will sit again at 9.45 tomorrow morning. I think it might be sensible to start in closed session and deal with all the matters that we can in closed session about the witnesses, and as soon as possible, if it is, we will move into open session. We will start in closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of April, 1999, at 9.45 a.m. 24 25
